body:
We make Kiron, so weigh this accordingly. Everything here about the other apps comes from their App Store listings, their own help and pricing pages and independent reviews, checked November 15, 2026. Everything about Kiron describes version 1.2.

Workout apps are usually compared feature by feature, but one question sorts them faster: who writes the plan? Some apps expect you to write it and just record what you do. Some write a new workout every time you open them. Some hand you a coach's program. And a few are built to run a plan you already have, whether it came from a coach, a book, a website or ChatGPT.

Answer that first, then check three practical things: whether you run too, what you'll pay, and which phone and watch you use. Below are eight apps, grouped by the job each one does, with links to our longer comparisons where we've written them.

If you only read this part

  • You write your own routine: Hevy or Strong. Both have free plans.
  • You want the app to choose each workout: Fitbod, or Hevy Trainer, which comes with Hevy's much cheaper Pro plan.
  • You want a program someone else wrote: Boostcamp for a free library, StrongLifts for one beginner barbell program, Ladder for a coach and a team.
  • Running comes first and lifting second: Runna.
  • You already have a plan, or you lift and run in equal measure: Kiron (that's us).

Bottom line: pick by who writes the plan, then rule apps out on price, runs and phone.

Four questions that narrow it down

Who writes the plan? If you know what you do each session and just want to record it, a log is enough, and logs are cheap or free. If you'd like the app to decide, you want a generator. If you'd rather a coach decided, look at coach-written programs. If the plan already exists, in a chat window, a coach's PDF or a notebook, the job is getting it into an app without retyping it as dozens of routines.

Do you run, ride or swim as well? Most of the lifting apps here log cardio but don't build running plans, so race training ends up in a second app. Running apps can have the opposite gap: Runna's strength sessions, for example, are pre-built, and you can't swap individual exercises. If both matter to you, check which half each app actually plans.

What will you pay? Entry-level plans here run from free to $179.99 a year. Most list several prices on the App Store, so what you're offered can differ from what's below. Compare yearly plans with yearly plans, look for a one-time purchase if you'd rather not subscribe, and check whether a free trial wants your card.

Which phone and watch? Ladder has no Android app. The others run on iPhone and Android, but watch support varies a lot, from Apple Watch and Wear OS apps (Hevy and Fitbod) to none at all (Boostcamp, and Kiron, which reads heart rate from Apple Health or Health Connect after a workout).

Switching from an app you already use? Export your history before you cancel; our guide to exporting your workout history has the steps for each app. One kind of app this guide leaves out: follow-along video class apps, such as Nike Training Club, Apple Fitness+ and Peloton.

Log what you already do: Hevy and Strong

Hevy is a workout log with a social feed. Its free plan logs unlimited workouts, with up to 4 routines, 7 custom exercises and 3 months of charts. Pro, at $23.99 a year or $74.99 once, lifts those limits and adds Hevy Trainer (more on that below). It has Apple Watch and Wear OS apps, and it can import your history from Strong.

Strong is a fast, plain set logger with an Apple Watch app. Its free plan logs unlimited workouts with 3 templates, and Pro is $29.99 a year or $99.99 once.

Both are good at recording and charting what you lift, and neither schedules a running plan. A plan you already have goes in as routines you build by hand, one per workout day, so a plan that changes from week to week can outgrow a free plan's routine limit quickly. More in Hevy vs Kiron and our look at Strong and its alternatives.

Let the app choose each workout: Fitbod and Hevy Trainer

Fitbod builds each session from your history, your equipment and which muscles have recovered, and its recovery map counts some of the workouts other apps save to Apple Health or Health Connect. It has Apple Watch and Wear OS apps. There's no free plan: after 7 days free, it's $15.99 a month or $95.99 a year for new subscribers. If you have a plan of your own, the catch is that choosing is the point; its help center says edits to a suggested workout are replaced if the suggestion refreshes before you start. The full comparison is in Fitbod vs Kiron.

Hevy Trainer comes with Hevy Pro, at $23.99 a year. It builds a program from your goals, experience, equipment and schedule, and suggests when to add weight; Hevy calls it algorithm-based rather than AI.

Both suit someone who'd rather not plan at all.

Follow a program someone else wrote: Boostcamp, StrongLifts and Ladder

Boostcamp is a program library with a tracker. Its free tier includes 99 of its 132 coach-designed programs, the tracker, and as many programs of your own as you care to build, using a web builder that handles phases and can import a spreadsheet. Pro is $59.99 a year. It has no Apple Watch app, and it's built around strength rather than cardio. If you want a named coach's program without paying, start here.

StrongLifts is built around one program, a barbell 5×5, and works out the weight increases and deloads for you. Its support pages say it became subscription-only in 2025. It's $59.99 a year or $11.99 a month, with a 7-day trial on the yearly plan, and it has an Apple Watch app. See what changed at StrongLifts, and where to run your 5x5 now.

Ladder puts you on one of 23 coach-led teams. Your coach writes a new 7-day plan every Sunday, with video demos and audio coaching in your ear. Pro is $29.99 a month or $179.99 a year, the 7-day trial doesn't take payment details, and there's no Android app. See Ladder vs Kiron on price, Android and flexibility.

Running comes first: Runna

Runna is a running coach. It builds plans from 5K to ultra, with pace targets that adapt as you go, and sends the workouts to Apple Watch, Garmin and COROS watches. You can add strength sessions, but they're pre-built for runners, and you can't swap individual exercises or write your own. It's $19.99 a month or $119.99 a year. If your race is the priority and lifting is support work, Runna fits. If the lifting matters as much as the running, read whether Runna's strength training is enough if you lift.

Run the plan you already have: Kiron

Kiron is built for the job in this guide's title: following a plan, whoever wrote it, with your runs in it. On its Add a program screen, Import a plan takes the plan as pasted text, from ChatGPT, Claude, a coach or a website, or as a photo, and turns it into a dated program with sets, reps and rest, phases included. There's no PDF upload, so a PDF goes in as pasted text or a screenshot. If you don't have a plan yet, there are 36 ready-made programs, an AI builder that asks a few questions, and a blank plan to fill in yourself.

Every program runs on the days you pick, on a calendar. Runs, rides, swims and rows sit in the same plan as your lifting, with time and distance targets. When the day doesn't go to plan, Adjust today's workout shortens or lengthens the session, swaps exercises for what a different gym has, or adds extra work such as core or a cardio finisher, all with an Undo, and missed workouts can be moved, pushed back or skipped. The recovery map counts workouts that other apps save to Apple Health or Health Connect. If you're coming from Fitbod, Strong or Hevy, Kiron imports their CSV exports, so your history comes with you.

Where it falls short, plainly:

  • {{kiron:free-tier-sentence}}
  • It has no Watch app; heart rate comes from Apple Health or Health Connect after the workout.
  • It needs a connection to open a workout.
  • Runs don't show pace, there's no social feed, and you can't export your history.
  • It's new, with a small user base.

{{kiron:pricing-sentence}} If your plan came from a chatbot, our guide to turning a ChatGPT workout plan into a program you can track shows how to check it before you start.

Questions people ask before picking one

Is there a free app for following a workout program?

Yes. Boostcamp's free tier includes 99 of its 132 coach-designed programs, plus a builder for your own. Hevy's free plan logs unlimited workouts with up to 4 routines, and Strong's allows 3 templates. A spreadsheet is free too, and for some people it's the right tool: here's when a spreadsheet beats an app. {{kiron:free-tier-sentence}}

Is there a workout plan app without a subscription?

Two of the apps here sell a one-time upgrade: Hevy Pro for $74.99 and Strong Pro for $99.99. Hevy, Strong and Boostcamp can also be used free, within limits. The rest are subscriptions: StrongLifts sells plans of up to five years, Fitbod, Ladder and Runna are monthly or yearly, and Kiron is {{kiron:price-weekly}} or {{kiron:price-annual}}.

Which workout planner apps work with Apple Watch?

Hevy, Strong, Fitbod, StrongLifts, Ladder and Runna have Apple Watch apps, and Runna also sends runs to Garmin and COROS watches. On Android watches, Hevy and Fitbod have Wear OS apps. Boostcamp and Kiron have no Watch app; Kiron reads heart rate from Apple Health or Health Connect after a workout.

Can I put a coach's or ChatGPT's plan into an app?

In most apps, you rebuild it by hand as routines or saved workouts. Boostcamp's web builder can import a program from a spreadsheet file. Kiron reads it as pasted text or a photo and schedules it on a calendar, phases included; a PDF goes in as pasted text or a screenshot.

What app handles running and lifting together?

If the race comes first, Runna, with its strength sessions as support work. If you want a full lifting program and your runs in one calendar, Kiron plans both. Either way, our post on running and lifting in the same week covers how to space the hard days.

If you already have a plan, or you want your lifting and your runs in one place, try Kiron with the plan you're following now. {{kiron:cta-sentence}} Get Kiron.

If you only need to log a routine you know by heart, start with Hevy's or Strong's free plan. If you want a free program library, Boostcamp is the place to look.
